name: Moshi
tagline: A small paid consumer productivity app whose public feature set is thin enough that the exact core loop needs verifying before you trust any clone estimate.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: We are not going to pretend to deep knowledge of this one: Moshi is a small independent app and its public surface is light, so treat this entry as a starting point rather than a ruling. What we can say generally: apps in this weight class are usually one person, one core loop, and a lot of polish, and a coding agent can reproduce the loop in a sitting. Where the weekend goes is everything around the loop, sync between devices, a real mobile or menu bar shell, notifications, and whatever OS permissions the app quietly handles for you. If the product turns out to lean on a proprietary model, a shared dataset, or hardware access, downgrade this to no. Until someone verifies the specifics, kinda is the honest answer.
coreLoopDIY: A local-first single-purpose app that reproduces Moshi's main interaction, storing everything in SQLite on your own machine with no account layer.
requirements: An OpenAI or Anthropic API key in .env only if the real product's loop is genuinely AI-driven
Willingness to read the actual product page before writing code
whatYouLose: Cross-device sync, which is the part nobody enjoys building twice
A native mobile or menu bar shell with proper permissions and background behaviour
The maintainer's taste: small apps like this are mostly the hundred decisions you would not think to make
Updates, so any OS change that breaks your build is now your weekend
Whatever hosted service or model the paid version quietly pays for on your behalf
moatNotes: Indie consumer apps rarely have a moat beyond feel and follow-through, which is a real moat right up until you stop caring how it feels.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a few dollars a month is cheaper than owning a piece of software. Small paid apps sell a finished thing: it launches, it remembers your settings, it works on your phone, and when macOS or iOS changes something under it, someone else fixes it. A self-built version gives you the loop and none of the maintenance contract, which is fine until the second week when the novelty wears off and you are debugging a permissions dialog instead of doing the thing the app was for. People pay to not be their own vendor.
notes: Low-confidence entry, flagged for verification: the verdict may move once someone confirms what Moshi actually does and what it charges.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal replacement for a small consumer productivity app.

Step 0, do this first and print your findings before writing code:
Fetch https://getmoshi.app/ and read it. In a file called SCOPE.md, write down: the single core loop the product sells, the three screens it needs, and anything that requires a real API, model, or OS permission. If the site is unreachable, stop and tell me instead of guessing.

Then build exactly what SCOPE.md describes, no more, using this stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 with the App Router and TypeScript
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/app.db, schema in one migration file
- pnpm, Node 20
- Runs with `pnpm dev` on localhost, single user, no auth

In scope:
- The core loop, end to end, working on first run with an empty database
- A list view, a detail or editor view, and a settings page that writes to the DB
- Full text search over stored records using SQLite FTS5
- Keyboard shortcuts for the two most frequent actions
- JSON export and import of everything, because this is my data
- A seed script that inserts five realistic example records

Out of scope, do not build these:
- Accounts, signup, billing, teams, sharing
- Telemetry, analytics, error reporting, any outbound call I did not ask for
- Mobile apps, native shells, push notifications
- Docker, CI, tests beyond one smoke test of the core loop

Rules:
- Any API key goes in .env.local and is read server side only; commit .env.example, never a real key
- If the core loop needs an LLM, use one server route, one model, and degrade to a clear error message when the key is missing
- No placeholder UI and no TODO comments: if you cannot finish a piece, delete it and say so

Finish with a README that lists the setup commands and one paragraph on what this build does not do compared to the paid app.
